publishedSummary: Every vessel wall is the same three layers in different proportions, and the proportions follow the job: elastic arteries to absorb the pulse, muscular arteries to distribute it, arterioles to regulate it, capillaries to exchange across it. Reading a vessel under the microscope is largely a matter of asking which layer dominates.
holdThese: A prominent internal elastic lamina marks a muscular artery; elastic arteries are the aorta and its large branches.
Many muscular arteries also show a recognisable external elastic lamina, and most medium-sized distributing and organ arteries are muscular.
The innermost layer of the endocardium is endothelium — continuous with the endothelium of every vessel.
Arterioles regulate flow into capillaries; exchange happens across capillaries and postcapillary venules.

Capillary type follows function: continuous in connective tissue, bone, skin and exocrine glands; fenestrated in intestine, endocrine glands and renal glomeruli, where glomerular fenestrae uniquely lack diaphragms.

sections.narrative:
The lining of the cardiovascular system is one continuous sheet. Inside the heart, the innermost layer of the endocardium is an endothelial lining, and it runs without interruption into the endothelium of the great vessels and onward to the smallest capillary. Everything else in a vessel wall is built around that sheet: an intima containing it, a muscular or elastic media outside that, and an adventitia anchoring the vessel to its surroundings.

What changes from vessel to vessel is which layer dominates, and that follows directly from what the vessel has to do. The aorta and its large branches are large elastic arteries: their media is loaded with elastic lamellae, so they distend during systole, store the ejected volume, and recoil during diastole to keep blood moving between beats. Further out, where the task is distribution rather than damping, the wall becomes muscular. Most medium-sized distributing and organ arteries are muscular arteries, and their media is dominated by smooth muscle whose tone sets the calibre of the vessel.

The boundary between the two types is what you actually look for down the microscope. A prominent internal elastic lamina, a distinct wavy line between intima and media, distinguishes muscular from elastic arteries — in an elastic artery the elastic material is spread throughout the media, so no single lamina stands out. Many muscular arteries also have a recognisable external elastic lamina at the media–adventitia junction, giving the muscular artery its characteristic appearance of a smooth-muscle sandwich bounded above and below by an elastic line.

At the far end of the arterial tree the wall thins until only the essentials remain, and the function changes from transport to control and then to exchange. Arterioles come first: heavily muscled for their size, they regulate blood flow to capillaries, and small changes in their tone produce large changes in downstream perfusion. Not all blood is obliged to make the capillary journey — arteriovenous anastomoses connect arterioles and venules directly, without capillary passage, allowing flow to be shunted past a bed entirely, as happens in the skin during thermoregulation.

Exchange itself happens where the wall is thinnest. Material exchange between blood and tissues occurs through capillaries and postcapillary venules — the venules are not merely drainage, but part of the exchange surface, and are also the site where leucocytes leave the circulation. Capillaries are not bare endothelium: pericyte processes usually surround the capillary endothelium, and because pericytes are contractile, pericyte contraction regulates capillary blood flow, providing a second layer of control beyond the arteriole. The same cell type persists just downstream, where the postcapillary venule wall contains pericytes and reticular fibres.

The endothelium itself comes in forms matched to the organ. Continuous capillaries, with an unbroken endothelial sheet, occur in connective tissue, bone, skin and exocrine glands — tissues where controlled, selective passage is what is wanted. Fenestrated capillaries, perforated by pores, occur in intestine, endocrine glands and renal glomeruli, wherever rapid bulk movement of water and small solutes is the point. The renal glomerulus takes this furthest: its capillary fenestrae lack the diaphragms found elsewhere, leaving an exceptionally permeable barrier — which is precisely what a filter needs to be.

If one generalisation is worth carrying out of this topic, it is that vessel type tracks position in the tree. Most medium-sized distributing and organ arteries are muscular arteries. Elastic arteries are confined to the aorta and its immediate large branches, where pulse damping matters; beyond that, the wall trades elastic lamellae for smooth muscle, because the problem has changed from absorbing a pressure wave to deciding where the blood goes.
